full_judgment:
5. The High Court Division failed to notice that a decree within the meaning of the Code of Civil Procedure means the formal expression of an adjudication conclusively determine the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may either be preliminary or final. In a suit for specific performance of contract, the court decides the controversy between the vendor and the vendee and direct the vendor to execute the deed in favour of the vendee if it is proved that the agreement is enforceable by law. It does not determine the title of the vendor in the property. It is true that in proviso to sub-section (l) of section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1885, no particular type of decree or order passed by a civil court at any time before the publication of the list has been mentioned. There is a reference as to any decree order passed by a civil court before the publication of the list in the gazette, but in view of the inclusion of the words 'declaring the building not to be an abandoned property .... to have been vested in the government...' there is no doubt about the intention of the legislature that unless a competent civil court passed a decree declaring the non-abandoned character of the building, the listing of the same cannot be said illegal. It is thus clear that the list shall not include any building if the decree or order is found declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not to have been vested in Government under PO 16 of 1972 or the possession by the Government of the building as abandoned property under that order to be illegal invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person. 

 6. As in a decree for specific performance, there cannot be any direction upon the Government to return or restore possession of the property or determine the title of the vendor, the inclusion of the building in the list does not invalidate the abandoned character of the building. There cannot also be a declaration in such a decree that the building is not abandoned property or that it has not vested in the Government under PO 16 of 1972. Reference in this connection is the case of CQMH Md Ayub Ali vs Bangladesh, 47 DLR (AD) 71. This decision has been approved by this Division in number of later cases. The High Court Division though noticed the said decision failed to appreciate the ratio of the same. 

 8. In the case in hand, not to speak of passing of any decree by anycivil court in respect of the disputed property, only a suit being Title Suit No. 142 of 1980 is pending in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract. Therefore, the case of the appellant is standing on a lesser footing than the one decided by this Division in CQMH Md Ayub Ali (Supra). The Court of Settlement upon assessment of the.materials on record came to a definite finding that Sakhina, Sultan and Nur Islam, the alleged predecessors of the appellant were not the actual lessees of the property under the Government. It was further held that though the appellant claimed to have entered into an agreement in respect of the disputed property with Sakhina Bibi and two others, she filed typed copy of the true copy of lease agreement and that she did not file the original copy of the same. She has not explained the withholding of the original lease deed. It was further observed that the appellant filed two pages of the agreement out of three pages and the photocopy of the same shows the agreement contains three pages. The agreement recites that possession of the building in question would be delivered in her favour after the execution of the sale deed. In view of the said statement, it was observed, her claim of possession falls through. The Court of Settlement also held that there is no legal evidence to show that Sakhina was living in Bangladesh. With these findings the Court of Settlement held that the application before it was not at all maintainable and that it was made with forged documents. The High Court Division has totally ignored those findings and decided the matter at its own volition as if it were on appeal from the judgment of the Court of Settlement.
